clue.text: Contract there could be money in it!

definitions.text: there could be money in it!

explanation.surface: A comment on a deal that might prove lucrative.
explanation.definitionFit: To purse the lips is to draw them tight, a contraction; a purse is the small bag that holds coins.

clue.text: Flat out writing about sharp rise

indicators.note: about means around, so the writing word goes around the rest

parts.note: prose is ordinary written language

indicators.note: in a down clue rise means going upwards, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: tart means sharp in taste

explanation.surface: A writer at full stretch describes a steep climb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rise' reverses TART to TRAT, which sits inside PROSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Prostrate means lying face down, stretched flat on the ground.

clue.text: Sack fathead in anger

indicators.note: in means the fat letter sits inside the anger word

parts.note: to rile is to anger or annoy
read as fat head, the head or first letter of fat

explanation.surface: Someone fires an idiot in a temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sack' reads as fire but means plunder; 'fathead' splits into the head of 'fat'.
explanation.definitionFit: To rifle a place is to ransack or plunder it.

clue.text: No longer an individual to esteem, that's clear

parts.note: ex means former, no longer what one was
one means a single individual
to rate is to esteem or value

explanation.surface: A former person to admire is now plainly vindicated.
explanation.definitionFit: To exonerate someone is to clear them of blame.

clue.text: A task soon disposed of in Canada

indicators.note: disposed here suggests letters set out in a new arrangement, so the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A quick job in Canada gets dealt with promptly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disposed of' looks like getting rid of the task, but it signals rearranging the letters of A TASK SOON; 'in Canada' defines a place there.
explanation.definitionFit: Saskatoon is a city in the province of Saskatchewan, so it is a place found in that country.

clue.text: Point a fellow put about this minute mount

parts.note: S, south, is a compass point
now means at this minute
a don is a fellow of a university college

explanation.surface: A man is set to work around the clock on a peak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put about' sets DON beside NOW. Snowdon is the highest mountain in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Snowdon is the highest peak in Wales, a mountain.

clue.text: A guy's entitlement has to be proven, holding him up

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the certain word wraps round the other

parts.note: sure means certain, proven true

indicators.note: in a down clue up means read from the bottom, so the word is backwards

parts.note: him is a man

explanation.surface: Someone's right must be shown, keeping a man waiting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses MAN to NAM, held inside SURE.
explanation.definitionFit: A surname is the family name a person is entitled to bear.

clue.text: Some popular songs give offence

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Certain pop hits cause upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'give offence' reads as cause upset, but here means an offence one commits, a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Arson, deliberate fire-raising, is a criminal act.

clue.text: Convertible proves disastrous it's just too much!

indicators.note: convertible means able to be changed, so the next word's letters are rearranged

parts.note: ill means bad or disastrous, as in ill fortune

explanation.surface: An open-top car turns out to be a calamity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convertible' looks like a car, but rearranges PROVES into OVERSP.
explanation.definitionFit: Overspill is the excess that runs over, more than can be held.

clue.text: One doesn't have to have them

definitions.text: One doesn't have to have them

parts.words: One doesn't have to have them
parts.note: read as a puzzle: things one lacks, the requirements one does not possess

explanation.definitionFit: Needs are wants or requirements, things one is without.

clue.text: Away from business, look gloomy and out of sorts

parts.note: off means away from, as in off work
CO is the abbreviation for company, a business
to lour is to frown or look sullen and threatening

explanation.surface: Someone on leave from work, moping and feeling unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling off colour is an idiom for being slightly unwell, not quite oneself.

clue.text: Picture causing a row?

explanation.surface: A question about an image that provokes argument.
explanation.definitionFit: A scene is a view or image; making a scene is a public fuss or quarrel.

clue.text: The subject for discussion is the state of Maine

parts.note: ME is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Maine

explanation.surface: Someone proposes Maine as the topic for a debate.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the topic a talk or essay treats.

clue.text: Patiently awaited conclusion

parts.note: read 'Patiently' as 'by patients': the verdict that people visiting a doctor wait to hear

explanation.definitionFit: A diagnosis is the doctor's finding about an illness, which a sick person waits to receive.

clue.text: Don't make a scholar turn colour!

indicators.note: turn tells us the word for a scholar is read backwards

parts.note: a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate scholar
to stain is to colour, as wood is stained

explanation.surface: An instruction not to force a learned person to change hue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' reverses BA to AB; 'Don't', as in 'I'd rather not', is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to refrain from doing something, such as voting or drinking.

clue.text: Stay to drink and drink

parts.note: to sup is to drink
porter is a dark beer

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to remain and keep drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stay' looks like a verb, but it is a noun: a prop.
explanation.definitionFit: A stay is a prop or brace holding something up.

clue.text: Involves a silent eccentric

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, so the letters of the words before it are jumbled

explanation.surface: Something requires a quiet, odd person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' looks like a noun for an oddball, but it rearranges A SILENT.
explanation.definitionFit: If something entails a consequence, it necessarily involves or brings it.

clue.text: Certain to get into step, which will be greatly appreciated

indicators.note: get into means enter, so the certain word goes inside the step

parts.note: a tread is a step, as on a stair
sure means certain

explanation.surface: A dance move, done right, will win applause.
explanation.definitionFit: Something treasured is held dear and highly valued.

clue.text: Energetic agent set about right and left

indicators.note: set about means placed around, so the agent word surrounds the rest

parts.note: a spy is a secret agent

explanation.surface: A busy operative attacks both left and right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set about' looks like attack, but puts SPY around RIGHT plus L.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprightly means lively and full of energy.

clue.text: Not stopping, say

explanation.surface: A note about a non-stop service, given as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: An express train runs without stops; to express a thought is to put it into words.

clue.text: Auster, the French cheat

parts.note: Auster is the Roman name for the south wind, S plus WIND
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A man called Auster and a French accomplice run a con.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auster' looks like a surname, but is the south wind.
explanation.definitionFit: To swindle is to cheat or defraud.

clue.text: Person arranging letters: for a tradesman without cash

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the tradesman word surrounds the cash

parts.note: a seller is a trader or dealer
P, a penny, stands for a little cash

explanation.surface: A trader with no money takes on someone sorting post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' reads as lacking, but here means outside: SELLER goes around P.
explanation.definitionFit: A speller puts letters in the right order to form words.

clue.text: Comes to respect the royal staff

indicators.note: comes to suggests turning into something else, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Esteem for the king's employees eventually arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' looks like employees but is a rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A sceptre is the ornamental rod a monarch carries.

clue.text: Standing by for a tedious party?

parts.note: something long is drawn-out and tedious
a side is a party in a dispute or game

explanation.surface: Waiting around, someone wonders if a dull gathering is coming.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand alongside someone is to be next to them, beside them.

clue.text: A bluff upstanding moralist

indicators.note: in a down clue upstanding means set upright, so the word reads from the bottom

parts.note: to pose is to put on a false front, a bluff

explanation.surface: An honest teacher of ethics calls someone's bluff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upstanding' looks like honest, but reverses POSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the Greek teller of fables, each with a moral.

clue.text: Raven's throat

explanation.surface: A note on a black bird's gullet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raven' is a verb, to eat greedily.
explanation.definitionFit: To gorge is to eat greedily, ravening; a gorge is also the gullet.

clue.text: Gave voice about inexperienced driver'sinsult

indicators.note: about means going round, so the singing word encloses the learner

parts.note: sang means gave voice to a tune
L is the learner plate shown by a driver still learning in Britain

explanation.surface: Someone shouted abuse at a learner driver.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a learner driver displays an L plate. SLANG as a verb, as in a slanging match, means to abuse verbally.
explanation.definitionFit: To slang someone, in British use, is to hurl abuse at them.

clue.text: Proficient, so likely to keep notes

indicators.note: keep means hold inside, so the likely word contains the notes

parts.note: apt means likely, as in apt to fail
D and E are musical notes

explanation.surface: A skilled student will probably take notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Adept means skilled, expert.

clue.text: Woodland character — a maker of trays

indicators.note: the answer, rearranged, makes up the word that follows, so its letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A forest figure turns out to be a craftsman of serving trays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a maker of' looks like a job description, but means the answer's letters can be rearranged to make TRAYS.
explanation.definitionFit: A satyr is a goat-like spirit of the forests in Greek myth.

clue.text: A cleaner put off by a vulgar fellow

parts.note: to deter is to put off or discourage
gent is a vulgar or jokey short form of gentleman, a fellow

explanation.surface: A housekeeper is repelled by a coarse man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vulgar' looks like it describes a coarse man, but labels GENT as an informal word.
explanation.definitionFit: Detergent is a cleaning agent such as washing powder.

clue.text: Continue always to be dressed in bluish grey

indicators.note: dressed in means clothed by, so the word for always goes inside the colour

parts.note: perse is an old word for a dark greyish-blue colour
ever means always, as in ever hopeful

explanation.surface: Advice to keep wearing grey-blue clothes for good.
explanation.definitionFit: To persevere is to keep going despite difficulty.

clue.text: Bats may be spotted

explanation.surface: A note that flying mammals might be seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' as an adjective means mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Dotty is slang for crazy; something dotty is covered in spots.
